questions.q: Why does the lesson say reconstructing run metadata (device, calibration state) after the fact is unreliable?
options: Because metadata is never provided by any quantum cloud platform
Devices recalibrate over time, so 'which device state did this run use' becomes unanswerable later if not captured at the time
Because providers delete all job records within an hour
Because reconstructing metadata is illegal under provider terms of service
questions.explain: The lesson explains that because devices recalibrate, the exact state used by a given run can't be recovered later unless it was recorded at the moment the run executed.

questions.q: How does the lesson say Lesson 4's interleaving principle should be applied when actually submitting jobs to a real queue?
options: Interleaving is impossible on real hardware and should be abandoned
Submit all of one condition's jobs first, then all of the other condition's jobs, in any order
Submit control/treatment or comparison-condition jobs close together in real time, rather than batching one condition days apart from the other
Always submit jobs to the device with the shortest queue, regardless of condition
questions.explain: The lesson translates the abstract interleaving principle into a concrete practice: submitting comparison-condition jobs close together in time (as in the worked run log, within a minute of each other) so both execute against a similar calibration window.

questions.q: What does the lesson say should happen if same-day execution of both comparison conditions turns out to be impractical due to queue behavior?
options: Report the result as fully controlled regardless of the queue delay
Document the limitation explicitly in the run log and later in the report's limitations section, rather than silently treating the comparison as controlled
Switch to a completely unrelated research question
Discard the entire experiment and start over with a new hypothesis
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit: if the controlled timing can't be achieved, that limitation must be stated honestly rather than hidden or silently assumed away.

questions.q: Which fields does the lesson's practical run log format include for each job?
options: The researcher's personal notes with no structured fields
Only the final computed probability for each run
Run ID, submitted/executed timestamps, device, calibration timestamp, circuit identifier, shot count, and data path
Only the device name, with no timing information
questions.explain: The worked run log table includes exactly these fields -- enabling later diagnosis and honest reporting of exactly what ran, when, and where the data lives.

questions.q: If a device goes offline mid-project and you finish runs on a different (same-model) device, what does this lesson say you should do?
options: Record the device switch in the run log and disclose it as a real limitation in the final report, rather than treating all runs as if they came from one unbroken condition
Discard all previously collected data and claim the project never happened
Hide the device switch since reporting it would make the project look unprofessional
Assume the switch has zero effect and make no note of it anywhere
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames unplanned device changes, queue variability, and maintenance outages as real operating conditions that should be documented honestly, not hidden or ignored.
